objects.ambiguityNotes: Computer animation appeared in earlier shorts and effects; this date marks the first fully computer-animated feature.
objects.funFact: Toy Story changed movie history by making a whole feature film with computer animation.

objects.name: SpongeBob SquarePants
objects.kidDefinition: A cheerful sea sponge whose friends turn ordinary days under the sea into silly adventures.
objects.dateBasis: SpongeBob SquarePants premieres on Nickelodeon.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the television series premiere, before later films, games, and books.
objects.funFact: SpongeBob’s world turned a pineapple, a burger job, and an underwater town into a long-running cartoon universe.

objects.name: Frozen
objects.kidDefinition: An animated movie about sisters, a snow-powered queen, and learning how love can thaw fear.
objects.dateBasis: Walt Disney Animation Studios releases Frozen.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first film, before sequels, stage shows, and books.
objects.funFact: Frozen made a centuries-old fairy-tale idea feel like a modern musical adventure for a new generation.

objects.name: Spirited Away
objects.kidDefinition: An animated movie about a girl who enters a mysterious spirit world and works bravely to save her family.
objects.dateBasis: Studio Ghibli releases Spirited Away in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original Japanese theatrical release, before the film reached audiences in other countries.
objects.funFact: The film’s world is full of unusual spirits, but Chihiro’s courage and kindness help guide the adventure.

objects.name: Transistor
objects.kidDefinition: A tiny electronic switch that made modern radios, computers, and phones possible.
objects.dateBasis: The transistor effect is discovered at Bell Laboratories in 1947; the work receives the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first working transistor, not the later mass production of transistor radios and computer chips.
objects.funFact: Three scientists shared the 1956 Nobel Prize for the transistor effect, a tiny idea that changed everyday electronics.

objects.name: Integrated circuit
objects.kidDefinition: A computer chip that packs many electronic parts onto one small piece of material.
objects.dateBasis: Jack Kilby demonstrates a working integrated circuit in 1958; he receives the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first working integrated circuit, before modern processors and memory chips.
objects.funFact: A chip can hold a whole crowd of tiny electronic parts on a piece smaller than a fingernail.

objects.name: Optical fiber
objects.kidDefinition: Thin glass strands that carry information as pulses of light.
objects.dateBasis: The practical low-loss optical-fiber idea develops in the 1950s; Charles Kao receives the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the practical foundation, before long-distance internet fiber networks became common.
objects.funFact: An optical fiber sends messages as flashes of light through glass thinner than a strand of hair.

objects.name: Lithium-ion battery
objects.kidDefinition: A lightweight rechargeable battery used in phones, laptops, and electric cars.
objects.dateBasis: The rechargeable lithium-ion battery develops through work in the 1970s and 1980s and reaches the market in 1991; it receives the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the key high-voltage lithium battery breakthrough, before commercial lithium-ion products became common.
objects.funFact: The same battery family can power a phone, a laptop, and an electric car.

objects.name: Blue LED
objects.kidDefinition: An efficient blue light-emitting diode that helped make bright white LED lamps possible.
objects.dateBasis: Bright blue LEDs are developed in the early 1990s; the work receives the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the breakthrough blue LED era, not the invention of the first red or green LED.
objects.funFact: Blue LEDs helped make bright white LED bulbs by combining blue light with special light-converting materials.

objects.name: PCR test
objects.kidDefinition: A laboratory method that makes millions of copies of a tiny piece of DNA to detect or study it.
objects.dateBasis: Kary Mullis develops PCR in 1983; he receives the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the invention of the method, before PCR became a routine medical and research tool.
objects.funFact: PCR is like a molecular photocopier: it turns one tiny DNA clue into millions of readable copies.

objects.name: mRNA vaccine
objects.kidDefinition: A vaccine that gives cells a temporary message so the immune system can practice recognizing a germ.
objects.dateBasis: The first mRNA vaccines are authorized for widespread COVID-19 vaccination in 2020; the underlying discoveries receive the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first widespread public use, while the supporting research began decades earlier.
objects.funFact: An mRNA vaccine gives cells instructions that disappear after the immune system learns from them.

objects.name: Tic-Tac-Toe
objects.kidDefinition: A quick three-in-a-row game played with Xs and Os.
objects.dateBasis: Ancient three-in-a-row games are recorded long before the modern paper version.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date is an ancient ancestor marker; the familiar paper form has no single invention date.
objects.funFact: A game that fits in a tiny square can still end in a clever draw.

objects.name: Sudoku
objects.kidDefinition: A number puzzle where every row, column, and small box must contain each number once.
objects.dateBasis: Howard Garns creates the puzzle later known as Sudoku as Number Place in 1979.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the puzzle’s origin in the United States. It was renamed Sudoku in Japan in the 1980s and became globally popular in 2004.
objects.funFact: Sudoku began as a magazine puzzle called Number Place before its Japanese name became famous around the world.

objects.name: Crossword
objects.kidDefinition: A word puzzle whose answers cross each other in a grid.
objects.dateBasis: The first modern crossword puzzle is published in a newspaper in 1913.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the modern newspaper crossword, not earlier word puzzles.
objects.funFact: The first modern crossword was designed to look like a diamond-shaped word game.

objects.name: Minesweeper
objects.kidDefinition: A computer puzzle where number clues help you avoid hidden mines.
objects.dateBasis: The familiar Windows Minesweeper version spreads widely in the early 1990s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier computer mine-clearing games existed; this date marks the familiar version children encountered on PCs.
objects.funFact: A number in Minesweeper tells you how many mines are hiding in the neighboring squares.

objects.name: Mario Kart
objects.kidDefinition: A racing game where familiar Nintendo characters use items and silly shortcuts.
objects.dateBasis: The first Mario Kart game is released in 1992.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first Mario Kart game, not the earlier Super Mario series.
objects.funFact: Mario Kart made racing games feel like a party by letting players toss items at one another.

objects.name: The Lion King
objects.kidDefinition: An animated coming-of-age adventure about Simba, family, and finding his place in the circle of life.
objects.dateBasis: Disney releases the original animated film in 1994.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original animated film, before later remakes and stage productions.
objects.funFact: The Lion King became one of the best-known animated films in the world.

objects.name: Shrek
objects.kidDefinition: An animated fairy-tale comedy about an ogre, a princess, and an unlikely friendship.
objects.dateBasis: The first Shrek film is released in 2001.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first film, before sequels and spin-offs.
objects.funFact: Shrek made fairy-tale characters joke about the stories they thought they were trapped inside.

objects.name: Finding Nemo
objects.kidDefinition: An animated ocean adventure about a young fish and the family searching for him.
objects.dateBasis: Pixar releases Finding Nemo in 2003.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first film, before its sequel and related attractions.
objects.funFact: Finding Nemo turned a dangerous ocean journey into a story about family, memory, and courage.

objects.name: The Incredibles
objects.kidDefinition: A superhero family tries to live an ordinary life while secretly helping people.
objects.dateBasis: Pixar releases The Incredibles in 2004.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first film, before its sequel.
objects.funFact: The film asked what would happen if a whole superhero family had to work together.

objects.name: Godzilla
objects.kidDefinition: A giant monster from Japanese cinema who became one of the world’s most recognizable movie characters.
objects.dateBasis: Toho releases the first Godzilla film in 1954.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original Japanese film, before the many later versions.
objects.funFact: Godzilla began in a 1954 Japanese film and grew into a worldwide movie character.

objects.name: Plants vs. Zombies
objects.kidDefinition: A strategy game where plants defend a house from marching zombies.
objects.dateBasis: PopCap releases the original Plants vs. Zombies game in 2009.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first game, before later sequels and spin-offs.
objects.funFact: The game turns a backyard garden into a lineup of defenders against silly zombie invaders.

objects.name: Garfield
objects.kidDefinition: A lasagna-loving orange cat from a newspaper comic strip who has big opinions about naps and Mondays.
objects.dateBasis: Jim Davis’s Garfield comic strip first appears in newspapers.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original newspaper comic strip, before television shows and films.
objects.funFact: Garfield’s very first comic-strip appearance was in 41 newspapers on the same day.

objects.name: Dog Man
objects.kidDefinition: A part-dog, part-police-officer hero who tackles silly mysteries with heart and lots of humor.
objects.dateBasis: Dav Pilkey’s first Dog Man graphic novel is published by Scholastic.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Dog Man appeared in an earlier Captain Underpants joke comic; this date marks the start of the Dog Man book series.
objects.funFact: Dog Man’s stories mix comic-book action, flip-book animation, friendship, and very silly jokes.

objects.name: Teddy bear
objects.kidDefinition: A soft toy bear made for hugging, comforting, and imaginative play.
objects.dateBasis: Toy makers create teddy bears during the Theodore Roosevelt bear story and craze.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Toy bears existed earlier; this date marks the named teddy-bear form that spread widely.
objects.funFact: The teddy bear’s name came from a nickname for President Theodore Roosevelt.

objects.name: Hot Wheels
objects.kidDefinition: Small toy cars made for racing, jumping, and zooming around tracks.
objects.dateBasis: Mattel releases the first Hot Wheels cars.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Toy cars existed earlier; this date marks the fast, track-friendly Hot Wheels format.
objects.funFact: The first Hot Wheels cars were designed with special wheels so they could roll quickly on tracks.

objects.name: Nerf
objects.kidDefinition: Soft foam toys and blasters made for playful games with less-stingy projectiles.
objects.dateBasis: Hasbro introduces the Nerf foam ball.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the original foam-ball toy; later blasters and foam darts came afterward.
objects.funFact: The first Nerf product was a soft indoor ball that could be thrown without breaking lamps.

objects.name: Transformers
objects.kidDefinition: Robot toys that can change into vehicles, animals, or other shapes.
objects.dateBasis: Transformers robot-to-vehicle toys debut alongside cartoons and comics.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Transforming toys existed earlier; this date marks the iconic robot-and-story universe.
objects.funFact: Transformers helped make changing a toy from robot to vehicle part of the play itself.

objects.name: Tamagotchi
objects.kidDefinition: A tiny digital pet that needs regular care, feeding, and attention.
objects.dateBasis: Bandai releases Tamagotchi in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electronic games came earlier; this date marks the pocket digital-pet format.
objects.funFact: A Tamagotchi made a tiny creature’s needs feel like a daily responsibility in your pocket.

objects.name: Clue
objects.kidDefinition: A mystery board game where players use clues to solve who did it, where, and with what.
objects.dateBasis: Waddingtons publishes Cluedo, known as Clue in North America.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first commercial edition of the mystery deduction board game.
objects.funFact: Clue turns a board game into a tiny detective story that players solve together.

objects.name: Risk
objects.kidDefinition: A strategy board game where players move armies and try to control a world map.
objects.dateBasis: Parker Brothers publishes the American edition of Risk.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The game first appeared in France as La Conquête du Monde; this date marks the familiar Risk edition.
objects.funFact: Risk turns a map of the world into a game of alliances, daring attacks, and changing plans.

objects.name: Dungeons & Dragons
objects.kidDefinition: A tabletop game where players imagine heroes, make choices, and tell an adventure together.
objects.dateBasis: The first Dungeons & Dragons boxed set is published.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Fantasy role-playing ideas were tested earlier; this date marks the first published D&D game.
objects.funFact: In D&D, the players help invent the story instead of following one fixed path.

objects.name: Magic: The Gathering
objects.kidDefinition: A collectible card game where players build decks and cast spells against each other.
objects.dateBasis: Wizards of the Coast publishes the first Magic: The Gathering set.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first widely recognized collectible trading-card game of its kind.
objects.funFact: Magic made a deck of cards feel like a personal toolbox of spells, creatures, and surprises.

objects.name: Yu-Gi-Oh! Trading Card Game
objects.kidDefinition: A strategy card game where players summon monsters, cast spells, and try to outsmart an opponent.
objects.dateBasis: Konami releases the Yu-Gi-Oh! Official Card Game in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The manga and animated story came first; this date marks the physical trading-card game.
objects.funFact: Yu-Gi-Oh! turned a fictional card battle from a story into a real game children could play.

objects.name: Tetris
objects.kidDefinition: A puzzle game where falling shapes must fit together to clear complete rows.
objects.dateBasis: Alexey Pajitnov creates the first Tetris computer game.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The game spread through different computers before its famous handheld versions.
objects.funFact: Tetris pieces keep falling, so the puzzle gets harder even though the rules stay simple.

objects.name: The Legend of Zelda
objects.kidDefinition: An adventure game where a hero explores a fantasy world, solves puzzles, and rescues a kingdom.
objects.dateBasis: Nintendo releases the first The Legend of Zelda game in Japan.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This date marks the first Zelda game, before its many sequels and spin-offs.
objects.funFact: The first Zelda game let players explore and discover much of the adventure in their own order.

objects.name: The Sims
objects.kidDefinition: A life-simulation game where players guide virtual people through homes, jobs, friendships, and everyday choices.
objects.dateBasis: Maxis releases the first The Sims game for personal computers.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Life-simulation experiments came earlier; this date marks the globally popular everyday-life sandbox.
objects.funFact: The Sims made ordinary chores, decorating, and neighbor drama into the main events of a game.

objects.name: Roblox
objects.kidDefinition: An online platform where people play and create many different user-made games and worlds.
objects.dateBasis: Roblox launches its online game-creation platform.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Online game communities came earlier; this date marks the platform built around user-created worlds.
objects.funFact: Roblox is less like one game and more like a huge shelf of games made by its players.

objects.name: Fortnite
objects.kidDefinition: An online game universe known for building, colorful events, and large multiplayer battles.
objects.dateBasis: Fortnite launches its first major game modes and later becomes a global multiplayer phenomenon.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The original Save the World mode came before the later Battle Royale explosion; this date marks Fortnite’s launch era.
objects.funFact: Fortnite turned a game into a changing online world with concerts, events, and new rules over time.

objects.name: Paper towel
objects.kidDefinition: An absorbent sheet of paper used to wipe spills or dry hands.
objects.dateBasis: Scott introduces paper towels in 1907.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Kitchen rolls followed in 1931; this entry uses the original paper hand towel.
objects.funFact: Paper towels reached public washrooms before they became kitchen rolls.

objects.name: Tupperware
objects.kidDefinition: Reusable plastic food containers with snug-fitting lids.
objects.dateBasis: Earl Tupper introduces Tupperware containers in 1946.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the named food-storage product, not the invention of plastic containers.
objects.funFact: Tupperware began with a bowl and a lid designed to seal in freshness.

objects.name: Plastic food wrap (Saran)
objects.kidDefinition: Thin, clingy plastic film that covers food and bowls.
objects.dateBasis: Dow launches Saran Wrap nationally for home use in 1953.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The material and industrial uses are older; this is the household food-wrap launch.
objects.funFact: Saran Wrap was Dow’s first consumer product.

objects.name: Resealable food bag (Ziploc)
objects.kidDefinition: A plastic food bag with a seal you can press shut and reopen.
objects.dateBasis: Ziploc begins selling its zipper-seal bags in 1968.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Plastic zipper patents and industrial bags came earlier; this is the familiar household product.
objects.funFact: Ziploc built its food bags around a reusable zipper seal.

objects.name: Aerosol spray can
objects.kidDefinition: A pressurized container that releases a mist when you press its valve.
objects.dateBasis: Erik Rotheim receives US patent 1800156 for his pressure-driven spraying container in 1931.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The US application was filed in 1927; this uses the patent grant, not wartime mass production or the earliest spraying experiment.
objects.funFact: Rotheim’s patent describes storing liquid and pressurized gas together in a spraying container.

objects.name: Battery-powered home smoke alarm
objects.kidDefinition: A small device that makes a loud warning sound when it senses smoke.
objects.dateBasis: Statitrol’s SmokeGard gains Factory Mutual approval and appears in the Sears catalog in 1972.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier commercial detectors and 1960s development preceded this affordable, self-contained home product.
objects.funFact: The SmokeGard could attach to a ceiling with just two screws.

objects.name: Electric garage-door opener
objects.kidDefinition: A motor-powered device that opens and closes a garage door.
objects.dateBasis: C. G. Johnson introduces an electric garage-door opener in 1926.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Overhead garage doors came earlier; radio remote controls came later.
objects.funFact: The electric opener followed Johnson’s overhead garage door.

objects.name: Blue jeans
objects.kidDefinition: Sturdy denim pants with pockets and metal rivets.
objects.dateBasis: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis receive their riveted work-pants patent in 1873.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Denim fabric and work trousers are older; the milestone is riveted blue jeans.
objects.funFact: Metal rivets helped strengthen the pockets of work pants.

objects.name: Rubberized raincoat
objects.kidDefinition: A coat with a waterproof layer that helps keep rain off your clothes.
objects.dateBasis: Charles Macintosh develops his rubberized waterproof cloth in 1823.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Oiled rainwear is older; this marks the material behind the recognizable mackintosh coat.
objects.funFact: Mackintosh coats use a rubberized layer to keep rain out.

objects.name: Canvas sneakers (Keds)
objects.kidDefinition: Light shoes with cloth uppers and flexible rubber soles.
objects.dateBasis: Keds introduces its Champion canvas sneaker in 1916.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Rubber-soled shoes and plimsolls are older; this is the iconic mass-market Keds product.
objects.funFact: Keds began with a simple canvas shoe called the Champion.

objects.name: T-shirt
objects.kidDefinition: A soft pullover shirt with short sleeves and no buttons.
objects.dateBasis: The US Navy formally includes the short-sleeved crew-neck undershirt in its uniform in 1913.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Similar undershirts existed earlier; this is a documented adoption milestone, not an absolute invention date.
objects.funFact: The T-shirt’s shape grew out of an undershirt.

objects.name: Hoodie
objects.kidDefinition: A sweatshirt with an attached hood to cover your head.
objects.dateBasis: Champion develops the hooded sweatshirt for athletes in the 1930s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Hooded clothing is ancient; Champion’s history gives a decade rather than a single invention year.
objects.funFact: The hoodie helped athletes stay warm on the sidelines.

objects.name: Baseball cap
objects.kidDefinition: A soft cap with a rounded top and a brim that shades your eyes.
objects.dateBasis: Brooklyn’s Excelsiors wear an early rounded-crown, projecting-visor baseball cap in 1860.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Teams wore other hats earlier; modern fitted and adjustable caps developed later.
objects.funFact: A baseball cap’s brim helps shade the player’s eyes.

objects.name: Mass-market sunglasses (Foster Grant)
objects.kidDefinition: Tinted glasses sold for everyday use in bright sunshine.
objects.dateBasis: Sam Foster sells sunglasses on the Atlantic City boardwalk in 1929.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Sun-shading eyewear is much older; this is a US mass-market sunglasses milestone.
objects.funFact: Foster Grant’s sunglasses business began on a seaside boardwalk.

objects.name: Wristwatch (Breguet’s)
objects.kidDefinition: A small clock worn on a strap or bracelet around your wrist.
objects.dateBasis: Breguet makes a purpose-designed wristwatch for the Queen of Naples between 1810 and 1812.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Use the commission-to-delivery range; earlier watch jewelry existed and everyday wristwatches became common much later.
objects.funFact: An early purpose-made wristwatch was created for a queen.

objects.name: Electronic digital watch
objects.kidDefinition: A wristwatch that uses electronics to display the time as numbers.
objects.dateBasis: Hamilton’s Pulsar electronic digital watch goes on sale in 1972.
objects.ambiguityNotes: A prototype was shown in 1970; mechanical watches with number displays are older.
objects.funFact: Hamilton called its electronic digital watch the Pulsar.

objects.name: Nylon school backpack
objects.kidDefinition: A lightweight fabric bag with shoulder straps for carrying books and supplies.
objects.dateBasis: Students adopt lightweight JanSport hiking packs for carrying books in the 1970s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Backpacks and nylon hiking packs are older; this decade marks their move into student life, not one inventor’s date.
objects.funFact: Hiking packs helped inspire the bags students carried to class.

objects.name: Instant coffee
objects.kidDefinition: Dried coffee that dissolves in hot water to make a drink.
objects.dateBasis: David Strang patents a soluble dry coffee powder in New Zealand in 1890.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Coffee concentrates and other soluble-coffee experiments existed; this is Strang’s documented dry-powder patent.
objects.funFact: Strang’s coffee powder could be made into a drink simply by adding boiling water.

objects.name: Corn Flakes (Kellogg’s)
objects.kidDefinition: Thin, crunchy corn cereal flakes often eaten with milk.
objects.dateBasis: W. K. Kellogg starts his commercial Corn Flakes company in 1906.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Flaked-cereal experiments came earlier; this is the familiar packaged product’s launch.
objects.funFact: Kellogg’s company began with the name Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company.

objects.name: Commercial peanut butter
objects.kidDefinition: A spread made by grinding peanuts into a smooth or crunchy paste.
objects.dateBasis: Commercial peanut butter emerges through Bayle’s and Kellogg’s products in the 1890s, with sales documented by 1897.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Ground-peanut foods are much older, and Edson patented a peanut paste in 1884; competing commercial origin claims require a range.
objects.funFact: Early peanut butter often separated into peanut solids and oil.

objects.name: Oreo
objects.kidDefinition: A sandwich cookie with two chocolate wafers around a sweet cream filling.
objects.dateBasis: Oreo launches in the United States in 1912.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the named cookie’s debut, not the invention of sandwich cookies.
objects.funFact: Oreo has appeared in different flavors around the world.

objects.name: Gummy bears
objects.kidDefinition: Small, chewy, bear-shaped fruit candies.
objects.dateBasis: Hans Riegel creates Haribo’s Dancing Bear gummy candy in 1922.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Other gummy sweets came earlier; the modern Goldbear’s shape developed later.
objects.funFact: Haribo’s original gummy bear was called the Dancing Bear.

objects.name: Quick-frozen food (retail)
objects.kidDefinition: Food frozen very quickly and kept cold until it is ready to cook.
objects.dateBasis: Birdseye’s packaged quick-frozen foods are test-marketed in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1930.
objects.ambiguityNotes: People froze food naturally long before this; Birdseye’s experiments and company also predate this retail milestone.
objects.funFact: Birdseye’s retail test included fish, meat, and vegetables.

objects.name: Chocolate-chip cookie
objects.kidDefinition: A baked cookie with little pieces of chocolate mixed into the dough.
objects.dateBasis: Ruth Wakefield’s chocolate-crunch cookie recipe appears in the 1938 edition of her cookbook.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The baking experiments may be earlier; this uses the documented published recipe, not the disputed accidental-invention story.
objects.funFact: The Library of Congress keeps a copy of Wakefield’s recipe book.

objects.name: M&M’s
objects.kidDefinition: Small chocolate candies covered in colorful, crunchy candy shells.
objects.dateBasis: Mars begins making M&M’s chocolate candies in 1941.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the original plain chocolate candy, not later peanut or other varieties.
objects.funFact: M&M’s started as chocolate inside a candy shell.

objects.name: TV Dinner (Swanson)
objects.kidDefinition: A frozen meal with separate foods in a tray that you heat and eat.
objects.dateBasis: Swanson introduces its branded TV Dinner in 1953.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Complete frozen meals existed in 1945; some histories emphasize Swanson’s 1954 advertising success.
objects.funFact: The tray kept the different parts of a meal in separate compartments.

objects.name: Frozen pizza
objects.kidDefinition: A prepared pizza stored frozen until you bake it.
objects.dateBasis: US commercial frozen pizzas appear in the 1950s, including a frozen-pizza patent application filed in 1950.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Several regional makers have origin claims; the decade avoids declaring one undisputed inventor. Totino’s mass production began in 1962.
objects.funFact: Frozen pizza let people keep an uncooked pizza ready in the freezer.

objects.name: Electric toy train (Lionel)
objects.kidDefinition: A miniature train powered by electricity that runs along toy tracks.
objects.dateBasis: Lionel begins producing its electric train equipment in 1901.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electric model trains existed earlier; this is the recognizable Lionel toy line’s start.
objects.funFact: Lionel’s first trains ran on two rails.

objects.name: Jigsaw puzzle
objects.kidDefinition: A picture cut into pieces that fit together to make the whole image.
objects.dateBasis: John Spilsbury’s dissected-map puzzles emerge in the 1760s; a surviving example dates to 1766.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Museum accounts use around 1760 or the surviving 1766 example; use a range instead of a false precise first.
objects.funFact: Early jigsaw puzzles helped children learn geography by fitting together maps.

objects.name: Matchbox cars
objects.kidDefinition: Small die-cast toy cars and trucks you can roll and collect.
objects.dateBasis: The Matchbox miniature-vehicle line launches in 1953.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Toy vehicles are much older; this is the distinctive pocket-sized product line.
objects.funFact: The toy’s size was inspired by a school rule allowing toys that fitted in a matchbox.

objects.name: Etch A Sketch
objects.kidDefinition: A drawing toy with two knobs that move a line across its screen.
objects.dateBasis: Ohio Art introduces Etch A Sketch in July 1960.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The French prototype came earlier; this uses the commercial toy launch.
objects.funFact: Etch A Sketch was the first Ohio Art toy promoted on television.

objects.name: Lite-Brite
objects.kidDefinition: A toy that makes glowing pictures with colored pegs on a lit board.
objects.dateBasis: The original Lite-Brite is produced in 1967.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Its development was inspired by a lighted window display in 1966.
objects.funFact: The original Lite-Brite came with 400 pegs in eight colors.

objects.name: Playmobil
objects.kidDefinition: Small toy people and themed playsets for making up adventures.
objects.dateBasis: Hans Beck and Horst Brandstätter present the first Playmobil figures in 1974.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the toy system’s debut, not the much older idea of miniature figures.
objects.funFact: The first Playmobil figures were presented at the Nuremberg Toy Fair.

objects.name: Regular radio broadcasts (KDKA)
objects.kidDefinition: Programs of news, talk, or music sent by radio for people to hear.
objects.dateBasis: KDKA begins regular broadcasts from Pittsburgh in November 1920.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Experimental broadcasts and other stations were earlier; this is a named regular-broadcasting milestone, not the invention of radio.
objects.funFact: KDKA’s regular broadcasting milestone happened in Pittsburgh.

objects.name: Color television (RCA CT-100)
objects.kidDefinition: A television set that shows moving pictures in color.
objects.dateBasis: RCA manufactures its CT-100 consumer color television in 1954.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Color demonstrations and other sets were earlier; this is a documented commercial color-TV model.
objects.funFact: The CT-100 was built at RCA’s plant in Bloomington, Indiana.

objects.name: Videocassette recorder (VCR)
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that records and plays video using tape inside a cassette.
objects.dateBasis: Sony launches its U-matic cassette video recorder in 1971.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Open-reel video recorders came earlier; home Betamax and VHS machines followed.
objects.funFact: U-matic machines were sold mainly to companies for training videos.

objects.name: DVD
objects.kidDefinition: A shiny disc that stores movies or computer information.
objects.dateBasis: Toshiba introduces its first DVD-Video player for Japan in 1996.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The standard was agreed earlier; other countries received players later. Use the first retail-launch year.
objects.funFact: A DVD is made by joining two thin optical discs back to back.

objects.name: Karaoke machine
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that plays backing music while you sing into a microphone.
objects.dateBasis: Shigeichi Negishi makes the Sparko Box karaoke machine in 1967.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Daisuke Inoue’s influential coin-operated machine followed in 1971; this uses the earlier IEEE-recognized machine.
objects.funFact: The Sparko Box used printed lyric cards instead of words on a screen.

objects.name: Electric guitar
objects.kidDefinition: A guitar that sends its string vibrations to an amplifier to make them loud.
objects.dateBasis: The Rickenbacker Frying Pan guitar is marketed in 1932.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier amplified instruments existed; this marks a successful guitar using an electromagnetic pickup.
objects.funFact: An early electric guitar was nicknamed the Frying Pan.

objects.name: The Muppets
objects.kidDefinition: Jim Henson’s group of funny puppet characters, including Kermit.
objects.dateBasis: Jim Henson’s Sam and Friends begins in 1955, introducing his early Muppets.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the early puppet ensemble, not The Muppet Show, which began in 1976.
objects.funFact: The early Muppets appeared in a short television program called Sam and Friends.

objects.name: Superman
objects.kidDefinition: A superhero from the planet Krypton who wears a cape and protects people.
objects.dateBasis: Superman debuts in Action Comics number 1 in 1938.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Use the first published comic appearance, not an earlier unpublished character concept or a movie.
objects.funFact: Superman’s first published adventure appeared in Action Comics.

objects.name: Spider-Man
objects.kidDefinition: A superhero who climbs walls and swings on webs as Peter Parker.
objects.dateBasis: Spider-Man first appears in Amazing Fantasy number 15 in 1962.
objects.ambiguityNotes: His own comic series starts in 1963; films and other versions are later.
objects.funFact: Spider-Man began as a high-school student juggling school and superhero adventures.

objects.name: Star Wars
objects.kidDefinition: A space-adventure world with Jedi, droids, starships, and the Force.
objects.dateBasis: The original Star Wars film opens in US cinemas on May 25, 1977.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Use the first film release, not story development, later episode numbering, or sequels.
objects.funFact: The original film is now also called A New Hope.

objects.name: Pencil sharpener
objects.kidDefinition: A tool that shaves a pencil’s wood and lead into a point.
objects.dateBasis: Thierry des Estivaux develops the familiar cone-and-blade pencil sharpener in 1847.
objects.ambiguityNotes: An 1828 patent used files; this entry chooses the recognizable modern blade design.
objects.funFact: The familiar small sharpener uses a blade inside a cone-shaped opening.

objects.name: Coloring book
objects.kidDefinition: A book of outlined pictures you can fill with your own colors.
objects.dateBasis: The Little Folks Painting Book is published in 1879.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is a documented early children’s coloring book intended for watercolors, not a claim about every earlier drawing exercise.
objects.funFact: Early coloring books could be filled with watercolor paint.

objects.name: Crayola crayons
objects.kidDefinition: Colored wax sticks used for drawing and coloring.
objects.dateBasis: Binney & Smith introduce their first box of eight Crayola crayons in 1903.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Wax crayons existed earlier; this is the named school-art product.
objects.funFact: The first box of eight Crayola crayons cost five cents.

objects.name: Comic book (early album)
objects.kidDefinition: A book that tells a story through a sequence of pictures and words.
objects.dateBasis: Rodolphe Töpffer publishes Histoire de Monsieur Jabot in 1833.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Picture stories are older; this is an early comic album, not the later American newsstand comic-book format.
objects.funFact: Early comic albums told stories through a sequence of illustrated scenes.

objects.name: Mass-market paperback (Penguin)
objects.kidDefinition: An inexpensive book with a flexible paper cover.
objects.dateBasis: Penguin launches its affordable paperback series in 1935.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Paper-covered books are centuries older; this is the influential modern mass-market series.
objects.funFact: Penguin aimed to make good books available at an affordable price.

objects.name: Whiteboard
objects.kidDefinition: A smooth writing board whose marks can be wiped away.
objects.dateBasis: Reusable white writing boards develop in the late 1950s.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Heit and Stallion have competing origin accounts; use a broad late-decade range. Dry-erase markers are a separate milestone.
objects.funFact: Whiteboards offered classrooms an alternative to chalk dust.

objects.name: Glue stick
objects.kidDefinition: Solid glue in a twist-up tube for sticking paper and card.
objects.dateBasis: Henkel launches the Pritt glue stick in 1969.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Liquid and paste glues are much older; this is the solid twist-up applicator.
objects.funFact: A lipstick tube inspired the glue stick’s twist-up design.

objects.name: Dry-erase marker
objects.kidDefinition: A marker whose ink wipes off a smooth board with a dry eraser.
objects.dateBasis: Pilot receives US patent 3912520 for dry-erasable writing-board ink in 1975.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Use this documented ink-patent grant, not a claim that all erasable markers began that year.
objects.funFact: The patented ink was designed to dry quickly but still wipe away without water.

objects.name: Smallpox vaccine
objects.kidDefinition: A vaccine that helps the body learn to fight the smallpox virus.
objects.dateBasis: Edward Jenner demonstrates successful smallpox vaccination using cowpox in 1796.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Variolation and earlier cowpox practices predate Jenner; this is the famous documented vaccination milestone.
objects.funFact: The smallpox vaccine used cowpox to help protect people against smallpox.

objects.name: Periodic table
objects.kidDefinition: A chart that organizes chemical elements into groups with shared properties.
objects.dateBasis: Dmitri Mendeleev publishes his periodic system in 1869.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Other element classifications came earlier; modern tables use atomic number rather than Mendeleev’s atomic weights.
objects.funFact: Mendeleev organized the elements into a repeating pattern.

objects.name: X-ray image
objects.kidDefinition: A picture made with X-rays that can show bones inside a body.
objects.dateBasis: Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays and makes radiographs in 1895.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the discovery and early imaging milestone, not the later development of routine hospital equipment.
objects.funFact: X-rays allowed scientists to examine the inside of the body.

objects.name: Aspirin (medicine launch)
objects.kidDefinition: A medicine used by doctors and adults for certain kinds of pain and illness.
objects.dateBasis: Bayer introduces the medicine under the Aspirin name in 1899.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Acetylsalicylic acid was synthesized earlier, and Bayer’s laboratory work dates to 1897; this is the medicine’s launch.
objects.funFact: Early Aspirin was supplied as powder in glass bottles.

objects.name: Insulin treatment
objects.kidDefinition: Using insulin medicine to help a person’s body control blood sugar.
objects.dateBasis: Leonard Thompson receives successful insulin treatment in Toronto in January 1922.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The research breakthrough was in 1921; this entry uses successful treatment in a person.
objects.funFact: One of the first people treated with insulin was a teenager.

objects.name: Vitamin C identified
objects.kidDefinition: Scientists working out which substance is vitamin C, a nutrient our bodies need.
objects.dateBasis: Vitamin C is identified chemically in 1932, with Charles Glen King’s report published in Science.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Szent-Györgyi had isolated hexuronic acid earlier; identifying its vitamin activity is the milestone, not inventing vitamin C.
objects.funFact: Scientists had to identify which substance in food supplied vitamin C.

objects.name: DNA double-helix model
objects.kidDefinition: A model showing DNA as two strands twisted together like a spiral ladder.
objects.dateBasis: Watson and Crick publish the double-helix structural model in 1953.
objects.ambiguityNotes: DNA had been known earlier; Franklin’s and Wilkins’s X-ray work contributed crucial evidence. This is a model, not DNA’s discovery.
objects.funFact: The model showed DNA’s two strands twisting around each other.

objects.name: Laser
objects.kidDefinition: A device that makes a very focused beam of light.
objects.dateBasis: Theodore Maiman demonstrates a working ruby laser in May 1960.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier theory and microwave masers preceded this first working optical laser.
objects.funFact: The first working laser used a synthetic ruby crystal.

objects.name: CT scanner
objects.kidDefinition: A machine that combines X-ray views into pictures of slices through the body.
objects.dateBasis: The first patient brain CT scan is performed at Atkinson Morley Hospital in 1971.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Public announcements followed in 1972 and whole-body CT later; this uses the first patient brain scan.
objects.funFact: An early CT scanner was designed specifically to scan the brain.

objects.name: MRI scanner (human-body prototype)
objects.kidDefinition: A scanner that uses a strong magnet and radio waves to make pictures inside the body.
objects.dateBasis: Damadian’s team builds the human-body-sized Indomitable MRI scanner in 1977.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Lauterbur’s imaging method and earlier small images predate this; clinical and commercial scanners followed. This is a prototype milestone.
objects.funFact: One early body-sized MRI scanner was named Indomitable.

objects.name: Handheld GPS receiver
objects.kidDefinition: A portable device that uses satellite signals to work out your location.
objects.dateBasis: Magellan sells its NAV 1000 handheld GPS receiver in 1989.
objects.ambiguityNotes: GPS satellites and larger receivers existed earlier; this is the commercial handheld product.
objects.funFact: Early handheld GPS users checked a schedule to see when enough satellites would be overhead.

objects.name: Webcam
objects.kidDefinition: A camera that shares pictures or video over a computer network.
objects.dateBasis: Cambridge researchers build a networked camera to watch a coffee pot in 1991.
objects.ambiguityNotes: It joined the web in 1993; 1991 marks its local-network predecessor, commonly called the first webcam.
objects.funFact: The first webcam project helped researchers check whether there was coffee in the pot.

objects.name: USB
objects.kidDefinition: A connection system for plugging devices into computers and supplying power.
objects.dateBasis: The USB 1.0 specification is introduced in January 1996.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the original standard, not later USB-C connectors or USB 2.0 speeds.
objects.funFact: The original USB standard included low-speed and full-speed connections.

objects.name: Wi-Fi (original wireless standard)
objects.kidDefinition: A way for devices to connect to a local network using radio signals.
objects.dateBasis: The original IEEE 802.11 wireless-network standard is published in 1997.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The Wi-Fi name, alliance, and major consumer breakthrough followed in 1999; earlier wireless networking also existed.
objects.funFact: The original standard allowed wireless data speeds of up to two megabits per second.

objects.name: Bluetooth (industry launch)
objects.kidDefinition: Short-range wireless technology that connects devices such as headphones and phones.
objects.dateBasis: Five companies form the Bluetooth Special Interest Group in May 1998.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Development began earlier; the first specification and consumer products followed. This uses the public industry-initiative launch.
objects.funFact: Five companies joined together to make Bluetooth devices work with one another.

objects.name: Portable MP3 player
objects.kidDefinition: A pocket-sized device that plays music stored as MP3 files.
objects.dateBasis: Saehan’s MPMan portable MP3 player reaches the market in 1998.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier digital audio players used other formats; this is the commercial portable MP3 milestone.
objects.funFact: Portable MP3 players carried music as computer files instead of cassette tapes.

objects.name: iPod
objects.kidDefinition: Apple’s portable digital music player for listening through headphones.
objects.dateBasis: Apple introduces the first iPod in October 2001.
objects.ambiguityNotes: MP3 players already existed; this is the named product’s debut.
objects.funFact: The first iPod was advertised as holding up to a thousand songs.

objects.name: Google Maps
objects.kidDefinition: A digital map service for finding places and planning routes.
objects.dateBasis: Google Maps launches for desktop computers in February 2005.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Mobile apps, Street View, and turn-by-turn navigation followed.
objects.funFact: Google Maps began as a desktop service.

objects.name: Kindle
objects.kidDefinition: Amazon’s handheld electronic reader for digital books.
objects.dateBasis: Amazon introduces Kindle on November 19, 2007.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Electronic books and other e-readers came earlier; this is the Kindle launch.
objects.funFact: The first Kindle could download books wirelessly.

objects.name: iPhone
objects.kidDefinition: Apple’s touchscreen phone, controlled with taps, swipes, and gestures such as pinching.
objects.dateBasis: Apple introduces the iPhone with a large multi-touch screen in 2007.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is the original iPhone’s launch, not the invention of the smartphone. IBM Simon was sold in 1994; touchscreens and multi-touch research also came earlier.
objects.funFact: The iPhone combined a phone, a music player, and internet features in one device.

objects.name: Subway railway
objects.kidDefinition: A railway that carries passengers through tunnels underneath a city.
objects.dateBasis: London’s Metropolitan Railway opens between Paddington and Farringdon in 1863.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This was a steam railway; electric underground trains arrived later.
objects.funFact: The first London Underground line linked Paddington and Farringdon.

objects.name: Modern Olympic Games
objects.kidDefinition: An international sports festival where athletes compete for medals.
objects.dateBasis: Athens hosts the first modern Olympic Games in April 1896.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The ancient Greek Olympics are much older; this entry explicitly means the modern revival.
objects.funFact: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens.

objects.name: Scheduled passenger airplane service
objects.kidDefinition: An airplane service that carries paying passengers on planned trips.
objects.dateBasis: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line begins scheduled passenger service in 1914.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier airship services existed; this specifically means scheduled passenger service by airplane.
objects.funFact: The early airline used a flying boat for its trips.

objects.name: Windshield wiper
objects.kidDefinition: A moving blade that clears rain or snow from a vehicle’s front window.
objects.dateBasis: Mary Anderson patents her effective windshield-clearing device in 1903.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The original device was manually operated; automatic and intermittent wipers came later.
objects.funFact: Anderson’s wiper could be operated from inside the vehicle.

objects.name: Parking meter
objects.kidDefinition: A machine used to pay for a set amount of parking time.
objects.dateBasis: The first Park-O-Meter is installed in Oklahoma City in July 1935.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier parking-control ideas preceded this public installation.
objects.funFact: The first parking meter stood on a street corner in Oklahoma City.

objects.name: Traffic cone
objects.kidDefinition: A brightly colored cone used to mark off an area or guide traffic.
objects.dateBasis: Charles Scanlon receives US patent 2333273 for his resilient conical safety marker in 1943.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The application was filed in 1941; later plastic cones differ from this rubber design.
objects.funFact: Scanlon designed a marker that could bend when struck.

objects.name: Drive-through restaurant
objects.kidDefinition: A restaurant where people order and collect food while staying in their car.
objects.dateBasis: Red’s Giant Hamburg opens in Springfield, Missouri, in 1947 with an early drive-through.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Drive-in restaurants are older and first-drive-through claims differ; use this named documented example.
objects.funFact: Red’s Giant Hamburg was located along Route 66.

objects.name: Enclosed shopping mall (Southdale)
objects.kidDefinition: A group of shops connected by shared indoor walking areas.
objects.dateBasis: Southdale Center opens in Minnesota in 1956 as an enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Covered markets and arcades are older; this is the modern suburban mall milestone.
objects.funFact: Southdale let shoppers walk between stores without going outdoors.

objects.name: Three-point seat belt
objects.kidDefinition: A safety belt that crosses your chest and lap and attaches at three points.
objects.dateBasis: Volvo delivers a car with Nils Bohlin’s standard-fit three-point safety belts in August 1959.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Earlier belts and patents existed; this is Volvo’s influential production-car design.
objects.funFact: Volvo’s first car delivered with the belts was a PV544.

objects.name: 911 emergency number
objects.kidDefinition: A short phone number used in the US to call for emergency help.
objects.dateBasis: The first US 911 call is placed in Haleyville, Alabama, in February 1968.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Other countries had emergency numbers earlier; 911 coverage spread gradually across the US.
objects.funFact: The first 911 call was placed in Alabama.

objects.name: Recycling symbol
objects.kidDefinition: Three arrows chasing one another in a loop to represent recycling.
objects.dateBasis: Gary Anderson designs the recycling symbol in 1970.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Recycling is much older; this dates the graphic symbol rather than the activity.
objects.funFact: The familiar recycling design forms a loop of three arrows.

objects.name: Skatepark
objects.kidDefinition: A place with ramps and smooth surfaces made for skateboarding.
objects.dateBasis: Surf City, an early purpose-built skatepark, opens in Tucson in 1965.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Other early parks and origin claims exist; this dates a named documented park, not an undisputed world first.
objects.funFact: An early skatepark in Tucson included a concrete runway for skaters.

objects.name: Panama Canal
objects.kidDefinition: A waterway through Panama that lets ships travel between two oceans.
objects.dateBasis: The Panama Canal officially opens in August 1914.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Construction began much earlier; this is the opening of the working canal.
objects.funFact: Ships could cross Panama through the new canal.

objects.name: Empire State Building
objects.kidDefinition: A tall New York City skyscraper with observation decks.
objects.dateBasis: The Empire State Building officially opens on May 1, 1931.
objects.ambiguityNotes: This is its opening date, not the start of construction in 1930.
objects.funFact: The Empire State Building has 102 stories.

objects.name: Mount Rushmore sculpture
objects.kidDefinition: Four huge US presidents’ faces carved into a mountain in South Dakota.
objects.dateBasis: Work on the Mount Rushmore sculpture ends and the project is declared complete in October 1941.
objects.ambiguityNotes: The mountain is ancient; this dates the sculpture, not the land or earlier dedications of individual faces.
objects.funFact: The sculpture shows the faces of four presidents.

objects.name: Sydney Opera House
objects.kidDefinition: A performing-arts building beside Sydney Harbour with large shell-shaped roofs.
objects.dateBasis: The Sydney Opera House formally opens in October 1973.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Performances began shortly before the official opening; construction and design were earlier.
objects.funFact: The first opera production began a few weeks before the official opening.

objects.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle
objects.kidDefinition: A battery-powered vehicle astronauts drove on the Moon.

objects.name: Space Shuttle
objects.kidDefinition: A spacecraft with a winged orbiter that could return to Earth and fly again.

objects.name: Mars rover Sojourner

objects.name: International Space Station
objects.kidDefinition: An orbiting laboratory where astronauts live and carry out experiments.
objects.dateBasis: The first ISS module, Zarya, launches in November 1998.
objects.ambiguityNotes: Permanent crews began living there in 2000; assembly continued for years. This is the start of the station in orbit.
objects.funFact: Zarya was the first piece of the station sent into space.

objects.name: Burj Khalifa

sources.claimSupported: Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland was published in 1865.

sources.claimSupported: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz was published in 1900.

sources.title: A. A. Milne’s Winnie-the-Pooh
sources.claimSupported: A. A. Milne’s Winnie-the-Pooh was published in 1926.

sources.title: The Little Prince
sources.claimSupported: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince was published in 1943.

sources.title: Charlotte’s Web

sources.title: Peanuts history
sources.claimSupported: Charles M. Schulz’s Peanuts comic strip began in 1950.

sources.title: The Cat in the Hat
sources.claimSupported: Dr. Seuss published The Cat in the Hat in 1957.

sources.title: Asterix history
sources.claimSupported: The first Asterix comic strip appeared in Pilote on October 29, 1959.

sources.title: Where the Wild Things Are

sources.publisher: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
sources.claimSupported: Toy Story was released in 1995 as the first computer-animated feature film.

sources.title: SpongeBob SquarePants history
sources.claimSupported: SpongeBob SquarePants launched in 1999 as a major children’s animated series.

sources.title: Frozen anniversary history

sources.claimSupported: Studio Ghibli lists Spirited Away as a 2001 film released in Japan on July 20, 2001.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Physics 1956
sources.claimSupported: The 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized research on semiconductors and the transistor effect.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Physics 2000
sources.claimSupported: The 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized Jack Kilby for his part in the invention of the integrated circuit.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Physics 2009
sources.claimSupported: The 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized Charles Kao for work on optical communication through fibers.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019
sources.claimSupported: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized the development of lithium-ion batteries.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Physics 2014
sources.claimSupported: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics recognized the invention of efficient blue light-emitting diodes.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1993
sources.claimSupported: The 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry recognized Kary Mullis for his invention of PCR.

sources.title: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023
sources.claimSupported: The 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognized discoveries enabling effective mRNA vaccines.

sources.title: Tic-tac-toe history
sources.claimSupported: Tic-tac-toe is a long-standing three-in-a-row game with ancient ancestors.

sources.title: History of Sudoku
sources.claimSupported: Howard Garns creates the puzzle later known as Sudoku in 1979, when it appears in Dell magazine as Number Place.

sources.title: Crossword history
sources.claimSupported: The first modern crossword puzzle appears in a newspaper in 1913.

sources.title: Minesweeper history

sources.title: Mario Kart history
sources.claimSupported: The first Super Mario Kart game was released in 1992.

sources.title: The Lion King
sources.claimSupported: Disney released the original animated The Lion King in 1994.

sources.title: Shrek

sources.claimSupported: Pixar released Finding Nemo in 2003.

sources.title: The Incredibles
sources.claimSupported: Pixar released The Incredibles in 2004.

sources.title: Godzilla history
sources.claimSupported: Toho released the first Godzilla film in 1954.

sources.title: Plants vs. Zombies
sources.claimSupported: PopCap’s original Plants vs. Zombies game was released in 2009.

sources.title: Milestones in Garfield History
sources.claimSupported: Jim Davis’s Garfield comic strip debuted in 41 newspapers on June 19, 1978.

sources.title: About Dav Pilkey
sources.claimSupported: The Dog Man graphic-novel series launched in August 2016.

sources.title: Teddy bear history
sources.claimSupported: The teddy bear became a popular toy in the United States around 1902.

sources.title: Hot Wheels history
sources.claimSupported: The first Hot Wheels car, the Custom Camaro, was sold in May 1968.

sources.title: Nerf history
sources.claimSupported: Hasbro introduced the first Nerf foam ball in 1969.

sources.title: Transformers 40th anniversary
sources.claimSupported: Transformers robot-to-vehicle toys debuted in 1984.

sources.title: Tamagotchi history
sources.claimSupported: Bandai released the original Tamagotchi digital pet in Japan in 1996.

sources.title: Clue board game history
sources.claimSupported: The Cluedo mystery board game was first published in 1949.

sources.title: Risk board game history
sources.claimSupported: Risk was first published in France and reached the United States in the late 1950s.

sources.title: Dungeons & Dragons history
sources.claimSupported: The first Dungeons & Dragons boxed set was published in 1974.

sources.title: Magic history
sources.claimSupported: The first Magic: The Gathering set was released in 1993.

sources.title: Yu-Gi-Oh! history
sources.claimSupported: The Yu-Gi-Oh! Official Card Game began in Japan in 1999.

sources.title: Tetris history
sources.claimSupported: Alexey Pajitnov created the first Tetris game in 1984.

sources.title: The Legend of Zelda history
sources.claimSupported: The first The Legend of Zelda game was released in Japan in 1986.

sources.title: The Sims history
sources.claimSupported: The first The Sims game was released for personal computers in 2000.

sources.title: Roblox about page
sources.claimSupported: Roblox launched its online user-created game platform in 2006.

sources.title: Fortnite history
sources.claimSupported: Fortnite launched in 2017 and grew into a major online multiplayer game universe.

sources.title: Paper towel: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Scott introduces paper towels in 1907. Paper towels reached public washrooms before they became kitchen rolls.

sources.title: Tupperware: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Earl Tupper introduces Tupperware containers in 1946. Tupperware began with a bowl and a lid designed to seal in freshness.

sources.title: Plastic food wrap (Saran): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Dow launches Saran Wrap nationally for home use in 1953. Saran Wrap was Dow’s first consumer product.

sources.title: Resealable food bag (Ziploc): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Ziploc begins selling its zipper-seal bags in 1968. Ziploc built its food bags around a reusable zipper seal.

sources.title: Aerosol spray can: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Erik Rotheim receives US patent 1800156 for his pressure-driven spraying container in 1931. Rotheim’s patent describes storing liquid and pressurized gas together in a spraying container.

sources.title: Battery-powered home smoke alarm: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Statitrol’s SmokeGard gains Factory Mutual approval and appears in the Sears catalog in 1972. The SmokeGard could attach to a ceiling with just two screws.

sources.title: Electric garage-door opener: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: C. G. Johnson introduces an electric garage-door opener in 1926. The electric opener followed Johnson’s overhead garage door.

sources.title: Blue jeans: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis receive their riveted work-pants patent in 1873. Metal rivets helped strengthen the pockets of work pants.

sources.title: Rubberized raincoat: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Charles Macintosh develops his rubberized waterproof cloth in 1823. Mackintosh coats use a rubberized layer to keep rain out.

sources.title: Canvas sneakers (Keds): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Keds introduces its Champion canvas sneaker in 1916. Keds began with a simple canvas shoe called the Champion.

sources.title: T-shirt: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The US Navy formally includes the short-sleeved crew-neck undershirt in its uniform in 1913. The T-shirt’s shape grew out of an undershirt.

sources.title: Hoodie: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Champion develops the hooded sweatshirt for athletes in the 1930s. The hoodie helped athletes stay warm on the sidelines.

sources.title: Baseball cap: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Brooklyn’s Excelsiors wear an early rounded-crown, projecting-visor baseball cap in 1860. A baseball cap’s brim helps shade the player’s eyes.

sources.title: Mass-market sunglasses (Foster Grant): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Sam Foster sells sunglasses on the Atlantic City boardwalk in 1929. Foster Grant’s sunglasses business began on a seaside boardwalk.

sources.title: Wristwatch (Breguet’s): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Breguet makes a purpose-designed wristwatch for the Queen of Naples between 1810 and 1812. An early purpose-made wristwatch was created for a queen.

sources.title: Electronic digital watch: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Hamilton’s Pulsar electronic digital watch goes on sale in 1972. Hamilton called its electronic digital watch the Pulsar.

sources.title: Nylon school backpack: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Students adopt lightweight JanSport hiking packs for carrying books in the 1970s. Hiking packs helped inspire the bags students carried to class.

sources.title: Instant coffee: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: David Strang patents a soluble dry coffee powder in New Zealand in 1890. Strang’s coffee powder could be made into a drink simply by adding boiling water.

sources.title: Corn Flakes (Kellogg’s): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: W. K. Kellogg starts his commercial Corn Flakes company in 1906. Kellogg’s company began with the name Battle Creek Toasted Corn Flake Company.

sources.title: Commercial peanut butter: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Commercial peanut butter emerges through Bayle’s and Kellogg’s products in the 1890s, with sales documented by 1897. Early peanut butter often separated into peanut solids and oil.

sources.title: Oreo: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Oreo launches in the United States in 1912. Oreo has appeared in different flavors around the world.

sources.title: Gummy bears: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Hans Riegel creates Haribo’s Dancing Bear gummy candy in 1922. Haribo’s original gummy bear was called the Dancing Bear.

sources.title: Quick-frozen food (retail): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Birdseye’s packaged quick-frozen foods are test-marketed in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1930. Birdseye’s retail test included fish, meat, and vegetables.

sources.title: Chocolate-chip cookie: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Ruth Wakefield’s chocolate-crunch cookie recipe appears in the 1938 edition of her cookbook. The Library of Congress keeps a copy of Wakefield’s recipe book.

sources.title: M&M’s: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Mars begins making M&M’s chocolate candies in 1941. M&M’s started as chocolate inside a candy shell.

sources.title: TV Dinner (Swanson): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Swanson introduces its branded TV Dinner in 1953. The tray kept the different parts of a meal in separate compartments.

sources.title: Frozen pizza: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: US commercial frozen pizzas appear in the 1950s, including a frozen-pizza patent application filed in 1950. Frozen pizza let people keep an uncooked pizza ready in the freezer.

sources.title: Electric toy train (Lionel): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Lionel begins producing its electric train equipment in 1901. Lionel’s first trains ran on two rails.

sources.title: Jigsaw puzzle: history and milestone
sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.claimSupported: John Spilsbury’s dissected-map puzzles emerge in the 1760s; a surviving example dates to 1766. Early jigsaw puzzles helped children learn geography by fitting together maps.

sources.title: Matchbox cars: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Matchbox miniature-vehicle line launches in 1953. The toy’s size was inspired by a school rule allowing toys that fitted in a matchbox.

sources.title: Etch A Sketch: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Ohio Art introduces Etch A Sketch in July 1960. Etch A Sketch was the first Ohio Art toy promoted on television.

sources.title: Lite-Brite: history and milestone
sources.publisher: The Strong National Museum of Play
sources.claimSupported: The original Lite-Brite is produced in 1967. The original Lite-Brite came with 400 pegs in eight colors.

sources.title: Playmobil: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Hans Beck and Horst Brandstätter present the first Playmobil figures in 1974. The first Playmobil figures were presented at the Nuremberg Toy Fair.

sources.title: Regular radio broadcasts (KDKA): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: KDKA begins regular broadcasts from Pittsburgh in November 1920. KDKA’s regular broadcasting milestone happened in Pittsburgh.

sources.title: Color television (RCA CT-100): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: RCA manufactures its CT-100 consumer color television in 1954. The CT-100 was built at RCA’s plant in Bloomington, Indiana.

sources.title: Videocassette recorder (VCR): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Sony launches its U-matic cassette video recorder in 1971. U-matic machines were sold mainly to companies for training videos.

sources.title: DVD: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Toshiba introduces its first DVD-Video player for Japan in 1996. A DVD is made by joining two thin optical discs back to back.

sources.title: Karaoke machine: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Shigeichi Negishi makes the Sparko Box karaoke machine in 1967. The Sparko Box used printed lyric cards instead of words on a screen.

sources.title: Electric guitar: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Rickenbacker Frying Pan guitar is marketed in 1932. An early electric guitar was nicknamed the Frying Pan.

sources.title: The Muppets: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Jim Henson’s Sam and Friends begins in 1955, introducing his early Muppets. The early Muppets appeared in a short television program called Sam and Friends.

sources.title: Superman: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Superman debuts in Action Comics number 1 in 1938. Superman’s first published adventure appeared in Action Comics.

sources.title: Spider-Man: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Spider-Man first appears in Amazing Fantasy number 15 in 1962. Spider-Man began as a high-school student juggling school and superhero adventures.

sources.title: Star Wars: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The original Star Wars film opens in US cinemas on May 25, 1977. The original film is now also called A New Hope.

sources.title: Pencil sharpener: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Thierry des Estivaux develops the familiar cone-and-blade pencil sharpener in 1847. The familiar small sharpener uses a blade inside a cone-shaped opening.

sources.title: Coloring book: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Little Folks Painting Book is published in 1879. Early coloring books could be filled with watercolor paint.

sources.title: Crayola crayons: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Binney & Smith introduce their first box of eight Crayola crayons in 1903. The first box of eight Crayola crayons cost five cents.

sources.title: Comic book (early album): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Rodolphe Töpffer publishes Histoire de Monsieur Jabot in 1833. Early comic albums told stories through a sequence of illustrated scenes.

sources.title: Mass-market paperback (Penguin): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Penguin launches its affordable paperback series in 1935. Penguin aimed to make good books available at an affordable price.

sources.title: Whiteboard: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Reusable white writing boards develop in the late 1950s. Whiteboards offered classrooms an alternative to chalk dust.

sources.title: Glue stick: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Henkel launches the Pritt glue stick in 1969. A lipstick tube inspired the glue stick’s twist-up design.

sources.title: Dry-erase marker: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Pilot receives US patent 3912520 for dry-erasable writing-board ink in 1975. The patented ink was designed to dry quickly but still wipe away without water.

sources.title: Smallpox vaccine: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Edward Jenner demonstrates successful smallpox vaccination using cowpox in 1796. The smallpox vaccine used cowpox to help protect people against smallpox.

sources.title: Periodic table: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Dmitri Mendeleev publishes his periodic system in 1869. Mendeleev organized the elements into a repeating pattern.

sources.title: X-ray image: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays and makes radiographs in 1895. X-rays allowed scientists to examine the inside of the body.

sources.title: Aspirin (medicine launch): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Bayer introduces the medicine under the Aspirin name in 1899. Early Aspirin was supplied as powder in glass bottles.

sources.title: Insulin treatment: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Leonard Thompson receives successful insulin treatment in Toronto in January 1922. One of the first people treated with insulin was a teenager.

sources.title: Vitamin C identified: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Vitamin C is identified chemically in 1932, with Charles Glen King’s report published in Science. Scientists had to identify which substance in food supplied vitamin C.

sources.title: DNA double-helix model: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Watson and Crick publish the double-helix structural model in 1953. The model showed DNA’s two strands twisting around each other.

sources.title: Laser: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Theodore Maiman demonstrates a working ruby laser in May 1960. The first working laser used a synthetic ruby crystal.

sources.title: CT scanner: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The first patient brain CT scan is performed at Atkinson Morley Hospital in 1971. An early CT scanner was designed specifically to scan the brain.

sources.title: MRI scanner (human-body prototype): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Damadian’s team builds the human-body-sized Indomitable MRI scanner in 1977. One early body-sized MRI scanner was named Indomitable.

sources.title: Handheld GPS receiver: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Magellan sells its NAV 1000 handheld GPS receiver in 1989. Early handheld GPS users checked a schedule to see when enough satellites would be overhead.

sources.title: Webcam: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Cambridge researchers build a networked camera to watch a coffee pot in 1991. The first webcam project helped researchers check whether there was coffee in the pot.

sources.title: USB: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The USB 1.0 specification is introduced in January 1996. The original USB standard included low-speed and full-speed connections.

sources.title: Wi-Fi (original wireless standard): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The original IEEE 802.11 wireless-network standard is published in 1997. The original standard allowed wireless data speeds of up to two megabits per second.

sources.title: Bluetooth (industry launch): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Five companies form the Bluetooth Special Interest Group in May 1998. Five companies joined together to make Bluetooth devices work with one another.

sources.title: Portable MP3 player: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Saehan’s MPMan portable MP3 player reaches the market in 1998. Portable MP3 players carried music as computer files instead of cassette tapes.

sources.title: iPod: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Apple introduces the first iPod in October 2001. The first iPod was advertised as holding up to a thousand songs.

sources.title: Google Maps: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Google Maps launches for desktop computers in February 2005. Google Maps began as a desktop service.

sources.title: Kindle: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Amazon introduces Kindle on November 19, 2007. The first Kindle could download books wirelessly.

sources.title: iPhone: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Apple introduces the iPhone with a large multi-touch screen in 2007. The iPhone combined a phone, a music player, and internet features in one device.

sources.title: Subway railway: history and milestone
sources.publisher: Transport for London / London Transport Museum
sources.claimSupported: London’s Metropolitan Railway opens between Paddington and Farringdon in 1863. The first London Underground line linked Paddington and Farringdon.

sources.title: Modern Olympic Games: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Athens hosts the first modern Olympic Games in April 1896. The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens.

sources.title: Scheduled passenger airplane service: history and milestone
sources.publisher: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
sources.claimSupported: The St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line begins scheduled passenger service in 1914. The early airline used a flying boat for its trips.

sources.title: Windshield wiper: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Mary Anderson patents her effective windshield-clearing device in 1903. Anderson’s wiper could be operated from inside the vehicle.

sources.title: Parking meter: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The first Park-O-Meter is installed in Oklahoma City in July 1935. The first parking meter stood on a street corner in Oklahoma City.

sources.title: Traffic cone: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Charles Scanlon receives US patent 2333273 for his resilient conical safety marker in 1943. Scanlon designed a marker that could bend when struck.

sources.title: Drive-through restaurant: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Red’s Giant Hamburg opens in Springfield, Missouri, in 1947 with an early drive-through. Red’s Giant Hamburg was located along Route 66.

sources.title: Enclosed shopping mall (Southdale): history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Southdale Center opens in Minnesota in 1956 as an enclosed, climate-controlled shopping mall. Southdale let shoppers walk between stores without going outdoors.

sources.title: Three-point seat belt: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Volvo delivers a car with Nils Bohlin’s standard-fit three-point safety belts in August 1959. Volvo’s first car delivered with the belts was a PV544.

sources.title: 911 emergency number: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The first US 911 call is placed in Haleyville, Alabama, in February 1968. The first 911 call was placed in Alabama.

sources.title: Recycling symbol: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Gary Anderson designs the recycling symbol in 1970. The familiar recycling design forms a loop of three arrows.

sources.title: Skatepark: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Surf City, an early purpose-built skatepark, opens in Tucson in 1965. An early skatepark in Tucson included a concrete runway for skaters.

sources.title: Panama Canal: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Panama Canal officially opens in August 1914. Ships could cross Panama through the new canal.

sources.title: Empire State Building: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Empire State Building officially opens on May 1, 1931. The Empire State Building has 102 stories.

sources.title: Mount Rushmore sculpture: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Work on the Mount Rushmore sculpture ends and the project is declared complete in October 1941. The sculpture shows the faces of four presidents.

sources.title: Sydney Opera House: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The Sydney Opera House formally opens in October 1973. The first opera production began a few weeks before the official opening.

sources.title: Lunar Roving Vehicle: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Apollo 15 astronauts first drive the Lunar Roving Vehicle on the Moon in July 1971. Apollo 15 carried the first car that astronauts drove on the Moon.

sources.title: Space Shuttle: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Columbia launches on STS-1, the first Space Shuttle orbital mission, in April 1981. The first orbital Space Shuttle mission was called STS-1.

sources.title: Hubble Space Telescope: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Hubble launches aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery in April 1990. A Space Shuttle carried Hubble into orbit.

sources.title: Mars rover Sojourner: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner land on Mars in July 1997. Sojourner explored a part of Mars called Ares Vallis.

sources.title: International Space Station: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: The first ISS module, Zarya, launches in November 1998. Zarya was the first piece of the station sent into space.

sources.title: Burj Khalifa: history and milestone
sources.claimSupported: Burj Khalifa is officially inaugurated on January 4, 2010. Burj Khalifa opened in Dubai in January 2010.

sources.title: Milestone matches at the FIFA World Cup
sources.claimSupported: The inaugural FIFA World Cup opened in Uruguay on 13 July 1930; thirteen national teams participated and Uruguay won the tournament.
